exam.title: MIT 6.0001: Computation, Branching & Bisection Search
exam.description: Undergraduate assessment on computational principles, Python types, branching, loops, and root-finding via bisection search.
exam.instructions: Answer all questions rigorously showing all work where applicable. Time limit: 60 minutes.

questions.text: In Python 3, what is the exact output of evaluating the following expression: `type(3 / 1)`?
questions.rubric: In Python 3, the single slash division operator (/) always returns a float object, even when dividing integers evenly (3 / 1 == 3.0).

questions.text: When using bisection search to find the square root of x in the interval [1, x] for x > 1 with precision epsilon, by what factor does the search space decrease in each iteration?
questions.rubric: Bisection search halves the search interval [low, high] in each step by choosing the midpoint, giving logarithmic time complexity O(log((high - low) / epsilon)).

questions.text: Explain why testing floating-point equality using `x == y` is dangerous in scientific computing, and describe the standard defensive programming approach taught in MIT 6.0001.
questions.correct_answer: Use abs(x - y) < epsilon instead of exact equality due to IEEE-754 binary representation rounding errors.
questions.rubric: Full credit requires mentioning that binary representation cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly (e.g. 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3), causing roundoff errors; and proposing testing |x - y| < epsilon with an appropriate tolerance.

questions.text:
Consider the code:
`s = 'mit ocw'`
`s[0] = 'M'`
What occurs when this code is executed?
options: TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
s remains unchanged with no error
questions.correct_answer: TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
questions.rubric: Python strings are immutable sequences; mutating an individual character directly raises a TypeError.
